content: Frankie Trull is an American advocate for science, a lobbyist, and an educator. She attended Boston University during the 1970s and later worked at Tufts University while pursuing a Master’s degree in sociology. During her time at Tufts, she was one of the founding members of the Research Animal Alliance, which eventually evolved into the National Association for Biomedical Research. This organization advocates for the use of animals in biomedical research and aims to represent its member institutions in national policymaking that impacts the use of animals in research, education, and product safety testing. In 1981, Trull established the Foundation for Biomedical Research, the largest organization in the United States advocating for the use of animals in biomedical research. The foundation was created to enhance public understanding and to counteract what she described as untruths propagated by animal rights activists. Currently serving as the president of the foundation, Trull is a vocal critic of direct actions taken against individuals or organizations that use animals for research purposes. In 2005, Trull compared the tactics of the Animal Liberation Front (ALF) to those of a classic terrorist organization. She characterized ALF activists as unbelievably mean-spirited people who operate under the delusion that they hold a higher moral ground than others. Trull has been recognized for her contributions to science advocacy. She was honored by the Society for Neuroscience and received the 2005 Award for Education in Neuroscience from the Association of Neuroscience Departments and Programs. In her award citation, she was commended for her efforts in promoting policies that support the humane and sensitive use of animals in biomedical research, ensuring that such work is not hindered. According to The Chronicle of Higher Education, Trull owns 16 horses, 4 cats, and a dog, all of which she considers to be members of the family.
